In Kubernetes, the chart configures Cluster Bootstrap with `DISCOVERY_METHOD=kubernetes-api`. ## What
Rejects deletion of an ingredient that is still referenced by a recipe line or a meal's direct-consumable line, instead of deleting it and leaving a dangling reference.

## Why
Deleting an ingredient out from under a reference left `GET /api/recipes` (which resolves every line's ingredient to compute nutrition) throwing a 500 for any recipe still pointing at the now-missing row. This was discovered live on the homelab deployment when a test-data cleanup deleted a referenced ingredient.

- `openspec/specs/ingredient-catalog/spec.md`: adds the requirement that deleting an ingredient needs no dependent references, with scenarios for an unreferenced ingredient, a recipe-referenced ingredient, and a meal-referenced ingredient.

Deleting an ingredient that is still referenced by a recipe or meal line leaves a dangling reference. ## What
Reject deletion of ingredients that are still referenced by recipes or meals to prevent broken nutrition resolution.

## Why
Deleting an ingredient that is still referenced by a recipe line or meal direct-consumable line leaves a dangling reference. When the system tries to resolve nutrition for those recipes or meals, it throws a 500 error trying to look up the now-missing ingredient. This was discovered in the homelab deployment when test-data cleanup deleted a referenced ingredient.

## Changes
- `openspec/specs/ingredient-catalog/spec.md`: Added requirement and three scenarios describing the deletion validation behavior (rejection when referenced, success when unreferenced)
- `server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/db/ingredient/IngredientRepository.scala`: Changed `delete` method signature from `Future[Boolean]` to `Future[Either[String, Unit]]`; added private `isReferenced` method that checks for recipe_line or meal_line references to the ingredient; deletion now returns `Left` with error message if referenced, `Right(())` on successful deletion
- `server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutes.scala`: Updated delete route handler to match on `Either` result, returning 400 BadRequest with error message on `Left`, 204 NoContent on `Right`
- `server/src/test/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutesSpec.scala`: Added two test cases verifying 400 rejection when deleting an ingredient referenced by a recipe line, and when referenced by a meal's direct-consumable line

## What
Rejects deleting an ingredient that is still referenced by a recipe line or a meal's direct-consumable line.

## Why
Deleting a referenced ingredient left it dangling, causing `GET /api/recipes` to throw a 500 when it tried to resolve that line's nutrition — discovered live on the homelab deployment after a test-data cleanup deleted a referenced ingredient.

- `openspec/specs/ingredient-catalog/spec.md`: adds the "Deleting an ingredient requires no dependent references" requirement with scenarios for unreferenced, recipe-referenced, and meal-referenced deletes
- `server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/db/ingredient/IngredientRepository.scala`: changes `delete` to return `Future[Either[String, Unit]]`, adding an `isReferenced` check against `recipe_line` and `meal_line` that rejects deletion when either references the ingredient, mirroring `BatchRepository.delete`'s discipline
- `server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutes.scala`: updates the `DELETE` route handler to match on `Left`/`Right`, returning `400 Bad Request` with an `ErrorResponse` on rejection instead of the old `true`/`false` NoContent/NotFound handling
- `server/src/test/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutesSpec.scala`: adds regression tests verifying `DELETE /api/ingredients/{id}` returns `400` when a recipe line or a meal direct-consumable line references the ingredient

## What
Reject deletion of ingredients that are referenced by recipe or meal lines to prevent breaking nutrition resolution.

## Why
Deleting an ingredient while it was still referenced by a recipe or meal line caused GET /api/recipes to throw a 500 error when trying to resolve that line's nutrition, discovered during live testing on the homelab deployment. This change prevents that failure by validating the dependency before deletion.

## Changes
- **openspec/specs/ingredient-catalog/spec.md**: Added "Deleting an ingredient requires no dependent references" requirement with three scenarios covering successful deletion of unreferenced ingredients and rejection when referenced by recipes or meals
- **server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/db/ingredient/IngredientRepository.scala**: Changed `delete` to return `Future[Either[String, Unit]]` instead of `Future[Boolean]`, added `isReferenced` query to check for recipe line or meal line references, and reject deletion with an error message if any references exist
- **server/src/main/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutes.scala**: Updated the DELETE endpoint to handle the new Either return type, returning BadRequest (400) with an error message when deletion is rejected and NoContent (204) on successful deletion
- **server/src/test/scala/me/cference/dionysus/http/IngredientRoutesSpec.scala**: Added two integration tests verifying that deletion is rejected when an ingredient is referenced by a recipe line or a meal's direct-consumable line

## What
Makes all three Hermes clients (Scala, JS, Python) treat a 2xx response as a successful delivery regardless of the response's `Content-Type` label, and adds a regression test to each client's suite covering this case.

## Why
A 2xx response whose body is valid JSON but arrives under an unexpected `Content-Type` header was at risk of being misread as a transport failure in the Scala client, since `Unmarshal` uses the content-type to select a decoder. Per the commit message and the `clients/README.md` update, misreading a delivered publish as failed causes retries and duplicate alerts; this was found in the wild by demeter-service.

## Changes
- `client/src/main/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClient.scala`: adds a private `asJson` helper that re-labels a `ResponseEntity` as `application/json` before unmarshalling, and applies it to every `Unmarshal(resp.entity)` call (get topic, list topics, publish, list subscriptions, pull, ack, modify ack deadline, health) so success is judged by HTTP status alone.
- `client/src/test/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClientSpec.scala`: adds a stub route for topic id `"plaintype"` that returns `202 Accepted` with a JSON body under `text/plain(UTF-8)`, and a test asserting the publish is still counted as delivered.
- `clients/js/test/client.test.js`: adds a stub handler for the `/plaintype/` publish path returning `202` with a JSON body under a `text/plain` content-type header, and a test asserting the publish result parses correctly.
- `clients/python/tests/conftest.py`: extends the stub server's `_send` helper with a `content_type` parameter, and adds a handler for topic `"plaintype"` that responds `202` with a JSON body under `text/plain`.
- `clients/python/tests/test_client.py`: adds `test_2xx_with_non_json_content_type_still_counts_as_delivered`, asserting the publish against the `"plaintype"` topic succeeds.
- `clients/README.md`: documents the new invariant — status decides success, not the body's content-type label — and notes it was found in the wild by demeter-service, with each client suite carrying an explicit test for it.

## What
Ensure clients judge delivery success by HTTP status alone, ignoring content-type headers on 2xx responses.

## Why
When a broker returns 2xx with valid JSON body but incorrect content-type header, clients were failing to parse the response and treating it as a transport failure. This caused delivered publishes to be retried, creating duplicates. The fix treats all successful (2xx) responses as JSON regardless of their content-type label.

## Changes
- **client/src/main/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClient.scala**: Added `asJson()` helper to re-label response entities as JSON before unmarshalling; applied to all `Unmarshal()` calls for successful responses across all API methods
- **client/src/test/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClientSpec.scala**: Added test case verifying publish succeeds when response returns 202 Accepted with JSON body under text/plain content-type
- **clients/README.md**: Documented that status decides success, not content-type label; explained the "Demeter trap" and added requirement that each client suite tests this case
- **clients/js/test/client.test.js**: Added test stub handler for plaintype topic returning 202 with JSON body under text/plain content-type
- **clients/python/tests/conftest.py**: Modified `_send()` helper to accept optional `content_type` parameter; added plaintype topic handler returning 202 with JSON body under text/plain content-type
- **clients/python/tests/test_client.py**: Added test case verifying 2xx with non-JSON content-type counts as delivered

response.output:
## What
HTTP clients judge response success by HTTP status code alone, relabeling response entities as JSON before unmarshalling to handle 2xx responses with unexpected Content-Type headers.

## Why
When a 2xx response contains valid JSON but arrives with an unexpected Content-Type header (e.g., text/plain), the client must still parse and count it as delivered. Misreading such responses as failures causes delivered publishes to be retried, resulting in duplicate messages — this has occurred in production (demeter-service).

## Changes
- `HermesClient.scala`: Add private `asJson()` method to relabel response entities as `application/json` before unmarshalling; apply it to all response parsing in getTopic, listTopics, publish, listSubscriptions, pull, ack, modifyAckDeadline, and health endpoints
- `HermesClientSpec.scala`: Add test case where publish to "plaintype" topic returns 202 with JSON body but text/plain content-type, verifying it parses and counts as delivered with the expected message ID
- `clients/README.md`: Document that success is decided by status code, not content-type label; note that each client suite has an explicit test for this behavior
- `clients/js/test/client.test.js`: Add stub server response for /plaintype/ topic returning 202 with text/plain content-type but JSON body; add test verifying it parses correctly
- `clients/python/tests/conftest.py`: Add optional `content_type` parameter to `_send()` helper method to support responses with non-JSON content types
- `clients/python/tests/test_client.py`: Add test verifying 2xx responses with non-JSON content-type still parse correctly

---
name: pr-description
description: Write pull request descriptions. Use when creating a PR, or when the user asks to summarize changes for a pull request.
---

# Role
You write the description for a pull request. A reviewer reads it before the diff, so it has to say what changed and why, accurately. You report what the diff shows; you don't guess at things it doesn't say.

# Task
1. Run `git diff main...HEAD` to see all changes on this branch, and read the commit subjects.
2. Write the description in the format below.

# Context
The description is used as the PR body exactly as you write it, so anything outside the format ends up in the PR. Reviewers use the Changes list to find their way through the diff, so each bullet should point them at the file it's about.

# Format
## What
One sentence explaining what this PR does.

## Why
Brief context on why this change is needed, taken only from what the diff, commit messages and code comments actually say. If they give no reason, say plainly what kind of change it is (for example, an automated dependency bump) and stop.

## Changes
- Bullet points of the specific changes made
- Group related changes together
- Each bullet names the file or files it covers and says what changed in them; every changed file appears in at least one bullet. For a new file, say what it contains
- Mention any files deleted or renamed

# Constraints
- Your reply is the PR description itself and nothing else. The first line is `## What` and the last line is the last bullet under `## Changes`. Don't put any sentence before `## What` (no "Here's the PR description"), don't add notes or a sign-off after the list, and don't wrap it in a code fence. `## Changes` contains only bullet lines.
- Name files the way the diff's file headers name them (a path or a file name). A class or function name is not a file name.
- Copy versions, numbers and identifiers exactly as the diff writes them.
- Don't guess what a new version, library or release may include, and don't add issue numbers, tickets or results the diff doesn't show.

## What
Makes the Scala Hermes client treat HTTP status as the sole signal of delivery success, re-labeling response entities as JSON before unmarshalling so a 2xx response with an unexpected `Content-Type` header still parses instead of failing; adds a matching regression test to all three clients' stub-server suites.

## Why
A 2xx response whose body is JSON but arrives under a non-JSON `Content-Type` label was being misread as a transport failure in the Scala client, which turns delivered publishes into retries and duplicate alerts (found in the wild by demeter-service, per `clients/README.md`). The JS and Python clients already parsed the body regardless of the label, so only their test suites needed the new case.

## Changes
- `client/src/main/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClient.scala`: adds a private `asJson` helper that re-labels a `ResponseEntity` as `application/json`, and routes every 2xx response body through it before `Unmarshal` (topic get/list, publish, subscription list, pull, ack, modifyAckDeadline, health).
- `client/src/test/scala/me/cference/hermesmq/client/HermesClientSpec.scala`: adds a stub route for topic id `plaintype` that returns a 202 with a JSON body under `text/plain(UTF-8)`, and a test asserting the publish still succeeds and parses.
- `clients/js/test/client.test.js`: adds a matching `plaintype` stub route (202, `content-type: text/plain`, JSON body) and a test asserting the publish result parses correctly.
- `clients/python/tests/conftest.py`: extends the stub handler's `_send` with a `content_type` parameter, and adds a `plaintype` route returning a 202 with `text/plain` content type and a JSON body.
- `clients/python/tests/test_client.py`: adds a test asserting a 2xx publish with a non-JSON content type still counts as delivered.
- `clients/README.md`: documents the "status decides success, not the body's content-type label" contract that all three clients' suites must test.

## What
Fix timestamp precision issue in ledger window comparison that causes all flyers to appear re-issued daily on Linux systems.

## Why
Postgres timestamptz columns store microsecond precision, while Java Instant stores nanoseconds. On Linux, Instant.now() populates the nanoseconds field, but on macOS it doesn't. When timestamps round-trip through the database, they lose sub-microsecond precision, causing raw equality comparisons to always fail on Linux. This made every flyer appear re-issued every day, resulting in ~9x unnecessary upstream requests to a bot-walled service, while the system appeared to work correctly.

- `FlyerLedger.scala`: Added `ChronoUnit` import and a new `truncate` helper function that truncates an Instant to microsecond precision (the database's actual precision).

- `FlyerLedgerSpec.scala`: Added a new test case that verifies flyers are not incorrectly re-selected after a database round trip, demonstrating the bug is fixed.

Postgres `timestamptz` stores microseconds while `Instant` carries nanoseconds, and Linux populates those sub-microsecond nanos while macOS does not — so a raw `!=` comparison between a stored window and an in-memory one was always true after a round trip. Fixes `FlyerLedger`'s window-change comparison to operate at the database's storage precision instead of in-memory `Instant` precision.

## Why
Postgres `timestamptz` stores microseconds, but `Instant` carries nanoseconds — and on Linux those nanoseconds are actually populated (macOS leaves them zero), so a round trip through storage truncates them. ## What
Fix ledger window comparison to operate at Postgres storage precision (microseconds) instead of Instant's nanosecond precision.

## Why
Postgres timestamptz stores microsecond precision while Java Instant stores nanoseconds. On Linux, Instant.now() populates nanoseconds, but Postgres truncates them on storage. A round-trip comparison between in-memory and stored timestamps was always false, causing every flyer to appear re-issued and be re-fetched daily (~9x upstream load). The bug was invisible on macOS (which doesn't populate nanos) and only failed on CI. Pre-truncating values on write and comparing at truncated precision makes the round-trip lossless.

## Changes
- **FlyerLedger.scala**: Add `truncate` function to truncate Instant to microseconds (ChronoUnit.MICROS), the precision Postgres can store. Update `shouldRefetch` to compare window timestamps at storage precision instead of raw equality. Update `PostgresFlyerLedger.recordFlyerFetch` to truncate timestamps before storing so the round trip is lossless.
- **FlyerLedgerSpec.scala**: Update the test's `now` value to explicitly include sub-microsecond nanoseconds to make truncation behavior deterministic across platforms. Update the existing window-from assertion to compare at storage precision. Add test "NOT re-select a flyer whose window survived a Postgres round trip" to verify the fix prevents unnecessary re-fetches.

Fix ledger window comparison to account for storage precision mismatch between Postgres (microseconds) and Java Instant (nanoseconds), preventing spurious re-fetches of every flyer daily.

## Why
Postgres timestamptz stores microseconds, but Java's `Instant` keeps nanoseconds—and on Linux actually populates them. The issue was invisible locally on macOS (where Instant.now() does not populate nanoseconds) and only failed on CI (Linux).

- `FlyerLedger.scala`: Added `truncate` helper function that truncates timestamps to microsecond precision (storage precision); added detailed comments explaining the precision mismatch and why truncation on the way in prevents data loss on round-trip

Postgres `timestamptz` stores microseconds while `Instant` carries nanoseconds, and Linux populates those nanoseconds while macOS does not — so a raw `!=` comparison between a stored window and an in-memory one was always true after a round trip, making every flyer look re-issued and get re-fetched daily. description: Write pull request descriptions. Use when creating a PR, or when the user asks to summarize changes for a pull request.

# Role
You write the description for a pull request. A reviewer reads it before the diff, so it has to say what changed and why, accurately. You report what the diff shows; you don't guess at things it doesn't say.

# Task
1. Run `git diff main...HEAD` to see all changes on this branch, and read the commit subjects.
2. Write the description in the format below.

# Context
The description is used as the PR body exactly as you write it, so anything outside the format ends up in the PR. Reviewers use the Changes list to find their way through the diff, so each bullet should point them at the file it's about.

# Format
## What
One sentence explaining what this PR does.

## Why
Brief context on why this change is needed, taken only from what the diff, commit messages and code comments actually say. If they give no reason, say plainly what kind of change it is (for example, an automated dependency bump) and stop.

## Changes
- Bullet points of the specific changes made
- Group related changes together
- Each bullet names the file or files it covers and says what changed in them; every changed file appears in at least one bullet. For a new file, say what it contains
- Mention any files deleted or renamed

- Your reply is the PR description itself and nothing else. The first line is `## What` and the last line is the last bullet under `## Changes`. - Copy versions, numbers and identifiers exactly as the diff writes them.
- Don't guess what a new version, library or release may include, and don't add issue numbers, tickets or results the diff doesn't show.
